The reason for these two gates is that all dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) possesses two meanings: first, the meaning of having power and lacking power; this refers to their functional efficacy.

Regarding the two meanings of having substance and lacking substance: in relation to this own-substance (*svabhāva*), by virtue of the former meaning, they attain mutual inclusion (*anyonya-anupraveśa*);

by virtue of the latter meaning, they attain mutual identity (*anyonya-ekatva*). In the former case, it possesses its own full power and is therefore able to encompass the other; whereas the other lacks any power whatsoever.
Thus they are able to enter one another. When the other has power and oneself lacks power, the opposite case can be understood accordingly.

Because it does not rely on its own substantiality, there is no identity (*samasvabhāva*). Because their functional powers (*śakti*) penetrate one another, they achieve mutual entry (*anyonya-praveśa*).

Furthermore, because the two states of having power and lacking power do not coexist, there is no absence of mutual non-entry; since the states of having power/lacking power and lacking power/having power are non-dual, they are therefore eternally [interpenetrating].
They mutually penetrate one another within the two kinds of emptiness and existence. This is because when the self-nature exists, the other must necessarily be non-existent;

therefore, the other is identical to the self. Why is this? Because the other lacks intrinsic nature and is produced by the self. Second, when the self-nature is empty, the other must necessarily exist; therefore, the self is identical to the other. Why is this?
Because the self lacks intrinsic nature and functions through the other. (One interpretation states: if one condition [is active], the others do not arise; their arising is not...)

If [the effect] were already established, the meaning of "condition" would be destroyed. Upon obtaining this single condition, the entirety of all things is established as arising; because that one arises and is established, the meaning of "condition" is finally established. Therefore, the single condition is the producer, while the multiple conditions and the fruit are both the produced.

Thus, many [conditions] constitute the establishment of one, and the many are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), whereas the one that produces the many possesses intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*). However, this point will be explained further later. This is because the two [existence and emptiness] do not coexist with each other.
Without that [other], there is no mutual identity; for existence and non-existence are neither existent nor non-existent, being non-dual. Therefore, they are eternally identical.

Furthermore, because the essence encompasses its function and there is no separate function, they are solely identical in appearance. If this were not so, dependent origination would not be established, and faults such as the existence of a self-nature (*svabhāva*) would follow;
these may be considered by examining them. Within this, regarding the mutual entry of light and form, there are two gates. First, the gate of...

Above, there are two directions leading downward; within the upward direction, there are likewise ten gates. First, the "one" is the fundamental number. Why? Because it is established through conditions.
This continues up to the tenth, where "within the one, there are ten. Why? Because if the one did not exist, the ten would not be established.
Thus, the one possesses full power and encompasses the ten; yet the ten are not the one. The remainder is now distinguished.

The nine gates are also like this; each has ten, which can be understood by following the same principle. (Master Yixiang said: "In the middle gate, 'going up' and 'coming down' refer to the interior of the gate;

'going up' and 'coming down' [in the sense of the exterior] are a confusion of terminology, and therefore they are not used. Within the ten numbers, there are also ten gates. First is "ten. Why? Because it is established through conditions.
... [omitted] ... Finally, "one" within the ten: if there were no ten, then one would not be established.
Therefore, the single [unit] lacks its own full power and returns to the ten; yet the one remains not the ten. The same applies to the remaining cases.
Thus, within these two gates of root and branch, all ten gates are fully contained. One should infer this for each of the remaining coins. (Regarding the method of numerical correspondence herein:

first is ten; second is nine within ten; and so on, up to tenth being one within ten. This is merely explained in terms of mutual comparison between different gates. Question: Since it has already been stated...
First: How can there be ten within one? Answer: This is the Dharma of the Great Pratītyasamutpāda Dhāraṇī. If there were no "one," then "all" would not be established;

therefore, it is known with certainty that this is so. What is the meaning of this? That which is called "one" is not a unity by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it is established through conditions.
Therefore, that there are ten within one is precisely being one through conditions. If it were otherwise, [it would not be so].

Self-nature has no conditions; it cannot be called "one. Therefore, all dependent origination is not self-nature. Why is this? Because if one condition is removed, everything ceases to exist. Thus, within the "one," many are contained; only then can it be called the "one" of dependent origination. Question: If removing one condition results in non-formation, then this is the absence of nature. That which lacks self-nature— [The text continues: ...is precisely what is called emptiness. Emptiness is the ultimate truth. It is because of this that all dharmas are empty. Since they are empty, there is no birth and no extinction. There is no coming and no going. There is no defilement and no purity. There is no increase and no decrease. This is called the Middle Way. To understand this is to enter the gate of the Dharma-realm. To practice this is to fulfill the path of the Bodhisattva. To realize this is to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, one should know that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent, beyond words and thought. This is the profound meaning of dependent origination. One who understands this is called a wise person. One who does not understand this is called an ignorant person. Thus, the Tathāgata has taught: "All conditioned things are like dreams and illusions; they arise from causes and conditions and have no inherent self-nature. This is the true teaching of the Buddha. One who hears this and believes with a single mind shall surely attain liberation. One who hears this and practices with diligence shall surely reach the Great Enlightenment. Therefore, you should all cultivate this with earnestness. Do not harbor doubt or hesitation. This is the essential core of the Mahāyāna. It is the supreme vehicle for crossing over the ocean of suffering. May all beings hear this and attain peace and joy. May all beings hear this and attain wisdom and insight. May all beings hear this and attain the unconditioned liberation. May all beings hear this and attain the eternal bliss of Nirvāṇa. How is it that the arising of the one and the many is established? Answer: It is established through the very absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Why is this?
Because this dependent origination is the true virtue of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and because the sphere of Samantabhadra possesses all virtues, is sovereign, and is without obstruction.
As the *Avataṃsaka* states: "The Bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the dharma of dependent origination; within a single dharma, he understands..."
They are numerous. Among these numerous dharmas, one understands a single dharma. For this reason, one should know that within the one there are ten, and within the ten there is the one;

they are mutually inclusive and unimpeded, yet they do not become identical to one another. Since the ten meanings are fully contained within a single gate, one knows that within each gate all meanings are inexhaustible.
It is the same for the remaining gates. Question: Within a single gate, are the ten meanings fully subsumed or not? Answer: [The ten meanings are fully subsumed.]
Exhausted or not exhausted? Why is this so? Because there is ten within one, it is exhausted; because there is one within ten, it is not exhausted. The four propositions protect the past;
they do not manifest virtues and so forth. This may be understood by analogy. Within each of the various gates, the application of the principle is likewise.
The subtle principle of dependent origination should be understood in this way. (The first section concludes.
Within the first section on distinct entities, the second concerns the meaning of identity; herein there are two subsections. The first proceeds upward.
The second is descending. Within the first gate there are ten gates. First is "one. Why? Because it is established through conditions. Up to the tenth is "one is ten. Why?
Because if there were no one, there would be no ten. Since the one has substantiality, the rest are all empty;
thus, this one is precisely ten. In this manner, ascending up to the tenth, all are likewise.
Each is as previously stated; they may be understood accordingly. Regarding what is called "descending," there are likewise ten gates.
First is ten. Why is this? Because it is established through conditions. And so on, up to: tenth is ten-in-one. Why is this? Because if there were no ten, there would be no one.
Since the non-substantiality of the one constitutes the existence of the others, these ten are therefore identical to the one. Thus, descending...
From the lowest up to the first, all are to be understood according to the preceding explanation.

For this reason, one should know that each single coin is itself many coins. Question: If one were not identical to ten, what fault would there be? Answer: If they were not identical, there would be two faults.
First, the fault that ten coins would not be established. Why is this? If one were not identical to ten, [the following would ensue].
Many ones also do not constitute ten. Why is this? Because each individual one is not ten. Since it is now established that they constitute ten, we clearly know that one is itself ten.
As for the fault that two ones do not constitute [ten]: why is this? If one were not itself ten...
The ten cannot be established. Because the ten are not established, the one meaning is also not established.
Why is this? If there were no ten, of what would the "one" be the one? Now that the one is attained, it is clear that the one is the ten.

Furthermore, if they were not mutually identical, then within the gate of dependent origination, the two meanings of emptiness and existence would not manifest, which would constitute a great error—namely, [the fallacy of] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth. Reflect on this.
This can be known. Question: If one is ten, it should not be one;
if ten is one, it should not be ten. Answer: It is precisely because one is ten that it is called "one. Why is this so?

As for what is called "one," it is not that which is termed "oneness" through the formation of a single condition (*ekapratyaya*) resulting in the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This is called "one" because this one is itself many;
if it were otherwise, it would not be called "one. Why is this? Because, due to the absence of intrinsic nature, there is no condition by which oneness could be established.
The principle that "ten is one" should be understood by analogy with the preceding example; do not hold false attachments. One should understand it accordingly.

Question: Regarding the meanings of "one" and "many" mentioned above, are they simultaneously and perfectly complete, or are they different in terms of sequence? Answer: They are both simultaneous and sequential. Why is this?
Because this *dharmatā* of dependent origination is fully endowed with both the reverse and the direct [order], being of the same essence and not contradicting its virtuous functions;
because it is sovereign and unobstructed, all things attain suchness. Question: Regarding the past and future as explained above...
[Question: What is the meaning? What are its characteristics? [Answer: It is that while remaining unmoved within its own state, it constantly comes and goes.

Why is this? Because coming and going are unmoving, as they are one and the same thing. It is merely for the sake of generating wisdom and manifesting the principle that the meanings of coming, going, and so forth are spoken of.
If wisdom were discarded, nothing at all could be expressed. This is precisely what is meant by the aforementioned "fruit-portion. [Question: If it is by means of wisdom...
If it is not previously existent, why do you say that it has been so from the beginning? Answer: If one sets aside wisdom (*jñāna*), then dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is not discussed.

It is by relying on wisdom that it is said to have been so from the beginning. Why? Because that which is unestablished is already [non-existent], and that which is established is free from beginning and end.
This is because both wisdom and the phenomena (*dharma*) have been established from the beginning. Question: Is it by means of wisdom, or is it the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatā*)?
Is this so? The answer is: Is it due to wisdom, or is it because the nature of phenomena (*dharma*) is such? Why? Because they are simultaneously and fully present.
Other meanings should be inferred accordingly. This concludes the explanation according to the section on the gate of distinct entities (*bhinnasvabhāva*).
Within the second section, the Section on Identical Substance (*tongti men*), there are also two meanings: first, the one within the many and the many within the one;
second, the one being the many and the many being the one. Within the first of these [two] gates, there are two: first, the one within the many; second, the many within the one.
Regarding "one in the midst of many," there are ten different aspects. First is "one. Why is this? Because it is established through conditions.
Within this fundamental number "one," all ten are complete. Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of these two coins is one, yet they also function as one with respect to the [other] two;
thus, they constitute "two-ones. This continues until, by functioning as one with respect to ten, everything constitutes "ten-ones. This is so.
Therefore, within this single "one," there are already ten "ones" inherent within it; yet, this one is not ten, because it is not yet the gate of identity (jimon).
Just as it is with the first instance of a single coin, so it is for each of the remaining nine gates from the second through the ninth;
this may be understood by following the same principle. Second, regarding the "one within the many," there are likewise ten gates. What are these ten?
For this reason, because they are established through conditions, one among the ten is [identical to them]. Why? Because by means of this one, the ten are made into one;
thus, that very first one exists within the eleven. Since there is no "first one" apart from the eleven, this one is precisely the one within the ten.
Yet, the ten are not the one. This applies to the remaining nine, eight, seven, and so on, down to...
One. All [numbers] are likewise so; reflect upon this by analogy. Question: What is the difference between this and the "distinct entities" (*bhinnasvabhāva*) mentioned previously? Answer:
Regarding the "distinct entities" mentioned previously, the first refers to a posteriority-based perspective when speaking of distinct gates. Within the second meaning, there are two gates:
first, "one is ten," which also has ten gates; this is not the same as the "one is one."
Why is this? Because they are established through conditions, one is ten. Why is this? Because these ten are precisely the first one;
they have no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, these ten are precisely one. The same applies to all the other nine gates.
This can be understood by analogy. Regarding the second point—that ten is identical to one—there are likewise ten gates. It is not that one is identical to ten. Why?
Because they are established through conditions; thus, ten is identical to one. Why? Because that first "one" is itself ten, and there is no separate, intrinsic "one.
Therefore, the first "one" is itself ten. The remaining nine gates should be understood by applying this same principle. Question: This...
Regarding the statement "within the same essence, one is ten, etc.," does this refer only to these ten, or does it encompass the inexhaustible?
The answer is that both follow the wisdom [of the practitioner]: when one requires ten, there are ten; when one requires the inexhaustible, there is the inexhaustible.
Such increases and decreases are taken according to wisdom. "Ten" is as explained previously. As for "inexhaustible," since there are already ten within a single gate, [the others follow suit].
However, these ten [realms] further mutually interpenetrate one another in layers upon layers, forming an inexhaustible whole.
Yet this entire inexhaustible, layered structure is entirely subsumed within the first gate. Question: Does it merely subsume the inexhaustible, layered structure within its own single gate?
"Are all [these] also subsumed within the other inexhaustible alternative gateways? Answer: "Either they are subsumed by both, or they are subsumed only by their own respective inexhaustibility.
Why is this? Because if there were no inexhaustibility within one's own single gateway, then the inexhaustibility within all other gateways would likewise fail to be established.
Therefore, the first gateway, being of the same essence, subsumes the inexhaustibility—without remainder—within both the gateways of sameness and difference."
(Up to ten layers) it exhausts the ultimate perfection of the Dharma-realm, such that there is nothing not fully encompassed.

Alternatively, it may encompass only the inexhaustible within its own single gate of identical essence. Why is this? Because other different gates are like space; because they do not cognize one another;
and because [this gate] is self-sufficient, there is nothing further to be encompassed. This merely takes one [gate] according to wisdom, without error or omission. It is thus.

Since each individual gate is fully endowed with infinity and inexhaustibility, as well as mutual identity and mutual inclusion, such that they constitute an inexhaustible whole, it should be understood by analogy that the same applies to every single gate;
each is inexhaustibly inexhaustible. This has been explained merely by way of the example of actual coins;
how much more so is this the case for the Dharma of the Inexhaustible Dhāraṇī of the One Vehicle’s Dependent Origination? It is not to say...
The Dharma is precisely like this. You should set aside all conceptual attachments and contemplate it according to its true principle.
As the Bodhisattva of the Forest of Diligence in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven said in verse:
"Just as in the method of calculation, One increases from one to the infinite; Yet the nature of the numbers has no inherent essence."

**Section on the Meaning of *Pratyaya* (Conditions):

Three Gates, same as before.** **First, the Explanation of the Name:** Dharma Master Lǐn said: "They mutually depend upon one another; thus they are called *pratyaya* (conditions). Conditions have no fixed abiding."

[The term] "clinging" [is used]. That the one and the many arise from conditions is called "arising. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Because there is no arising in equality, it is called 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Second, regarding the determination of its essence: the two masters Zang and Xiao take the unobstructed *dharmadhātu* as its essence; Master Lin says: "It is..."

The second is the essence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). One does not arise from one; rather, because two conditions exist, one arises. Two and one constitute one, and one and two constitute two; these serve as the essence of dependent origination.
As for what is called "one," it is neither existence nor non-existence; it is the single characteristic that is without characteristics. It is not that one becomes one.
As for what is called "two," it is the existence of non-existence and the non-existence of existence. This "existence of non-existence" serves to dismantle [conceptual extremes].

The non-existence of a rabbit’s horn is not a "non-existence" that negates the existence of empty space. To negate existence by speaking of non-existence—this non-existence is not [absolute] non-existence.
To negate non-existence by speaking of existence—this existence is not [absolute] existence. Because it is not existence, it exists yet is non-existent;
because it is not non-existence, it is non-existent yet exists. This existence and this non-existence are called "duality. Duality lacks the characteristic of duality; there is no duality.

And secondly. Third, the analysis through question and answer. Question: What is the meaning of "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? Answer: Some masters say that its meaning is as follows. One master who elucidates the characteristics says:
Dependent origination is non-discriminatory according to its nature; it is the identity of characteristics and the fusion of characteristics, which reveals equanimity.

The meaning of "equality" (samata) is that which correctly accords with the essence of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). As for "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya), they follow conventional distinctions;

that is, by viewing causes and conditions in relation to one another, they manifest the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). This is the essence of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

Second, Master Huiyuan of the Sui dynasty said: "The meaning of 'causes and conditions' (hetu-pratyaya) is also called 'dependent origination' (pratītyasamutpāda) and also called 'the gathering of conditions' (pratyaya-saṃgraha).

This means that all phenomena exist by relying on causes and depending on conditions; therefore, they are called 'causes and conditions. Because the arising of phenomena depends upon conditions, they are termed 'dependent origination.

Because phenomena gather from conditions, they are named 'the gathering of conditions. There are three distinctions: first, the conditioned (saṃskṛta); second, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); third..."

This is their intrinsic nature. That which is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) refers to the phenomena of birth and death; because its essence consists of impermanence and the processes of arising and ceasing, it is named "conditioned.

Because it exists through the causes and conditions of karma and afflictions, it is named "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*). That which is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) refers to what is known as *nirvāṇa*;
because its essence is not subject to arising and ceasing, it is termed "unconditioned. Because it exists by relying upon the Path, it is said to be "causes and conditions. This...
These two dharmas both arise from prior causes to produce subsequent effects; this is the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), these very dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are, in their own-being, entirely dependently originated. What is their characteristic? As it is said:
"The fundamental nature of saṃsāra is itself the Tathāgatagarbha. Within the Tathāgatagarbha, all [qualities] are fully present at all times.

The Buddha’s Dharma: these various phenomena share a single ontological nature (*ekasvabhāva*) and arise through mutual conditioning; not a single phenomenon exists that maintains its own intrinsic nature in isolation.
Although they possess this single nature, there is no lack of nature. Because there is no single [fixed] nature, all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*);

because there is no lack of nature, the gates of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are distinct. As it is with birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), so it is with nirvana; these phenomena of identical substance interact with one another.

Because they are gathered through mutual conditioning, it is called "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*). It is also termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and "the collection of dependent origination.
Within this very essence, there are further three aspects: first, the conditioned *tathāgatagarbha* (which is defiled by following delusion);
second, the unconditioned *tathāgatagarbha* (which is named pure because it is free from delusion); and third, the essential nature itself (which sets aside conditions to discuss reality).
Master Sanlin said: "The essence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is non-dual; its functions are opened up into four kinds: first, conditioned dependent origination;
second, unconditioned dependent origination; third, self-nature dependent origination; and fourth, dharma-realm dependent origination. This means that existence does not exist of itself;

existence arises through conditions from non-existence, which is called conditioned dependent origination. Non-existence does not exist of itself; non-existence arises through conditions from existence, which is called unconditioned [dependent origination]."

This is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) constitute duality; that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned is non-duality, serving as the fundamental essence (*svabhāva*).
This non-duality does not exist by itself as non-dual; rather, through the duality of dependent origination, there is non-duality. Furthermore, it is not self-originated; it arises from others.
Moreover, the essence is not self-essence; the essence arises through the function. Therefore, it is called "dependent origination of the self-essence. There is no duality.
The absence of duality is equality; both duality and non-duality constitute differentiation. Differentiation does not differentiate itself;
it arises from equality as its condition. Equality does not equalize itself; it is equality by virtue of differentiation as its condition.

That equality and non-equality are both entirely equal is called the dependent origination of the dharmadhātu. Question: What textual passage serves as proof? Answer: The *Lokātīta-stava* (Hymn to Him Who Transcends the World).
In one there are immeasurables; in the immeasurable there is one. Unobstructed and unimpeded. To summarize: all are dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
If there were even a single dharma that was not dependently originated, it would not be the Buddha-dharma. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"Deeply entering dependent origination, one cuts off all false views and the two extremes of existence and non-existence, because there is no longer any habituation [to them]. To know what is not dependently originated is not to strive."
[The section on] "Wrong Views" (and so forth).
The Master of the Four Dharma-Treasuries said: "Question: What causes and conditions allow these various dharmas to be thus interpenetrating and unimpeded?
Answer: The causes and conditions are immeasurable and difficult to describe in full; I shall briefly cite ten categories to explain this non-obstruction. First:

1. Because of the mutual conditioning of dependent origination; 2. Because the two natures are mutually penetrating; 3. Because each is manifested solely by the mind; 4. Because they are unreal like illusions; 5.
Because they are indeterminate as to size and quantity; 6. Because they arise from infinite causes; 7.

Because the qualities of the fruit are perfectly consummate; 8. Because of supreme supernormal powers and mastery; 9. Because of the great function of samādhi; 10. Because of inconceivable liberation. First.
Regarding the phrase "because of the mutual dependence of the characteristics of dependent origination" (the remaining nine gates are explained separately elsewhere, etc.), there are three gates:

first, the principle that all conditions are distinct from one another (also called the gate of the mutual difference of conditions; this refers to their distinct entities); second, the principle of mutual pervasion and reciprocal support (also called the gate of the mutual correspondence of conditions; this refers to their identical entity);

third, the principle of simultaneous existence without obstruction (also called the gate of unobstructed correspondence despite difference; this simultaneously clarifies both identity and difference). Regarding the principle that the combination of conditions is characterized by difference:

This means that when various conditions are compared with one another, it is necessary that their essence and function be distinct and not intermingled; only then does dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) come to be established.
If this were not the case, the conditions would be confused and disordered, the fundamental principle of conditions would be lost, and dependent origination would fail to be established.

This refers to the fact that each of these conditions maintains its own singular identity. Second, regarding the meaning of mutual pervasion and mutual support: it means that these various conditions must mutually pervade one another.

Only then can dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) be fully established. For instance, if one condition were to universally correspond with many conditions, each would be entirely identical to that one;

thus, this single one would possess multiple instances of "one. If this single condition did not possess multiple instances of "one," then the supporting factors would not be universal, and dependent origination would not be established.
Therefore, each and every one must individually possess all instances of "one. Thus, the three [conditions] coexist without exclusion.

Regarding the meaning of "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*): it means that for any single condition to constitute dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it must necessarily possess the two preceding [qualities].

This is because it must abide in its own locus in order to be pervasive, and it must be able to pervade multiple conditions in order to be singular. Therefore, the one and the many are sovereign and unimpeded.
These three sections above collectively clarify the fundamental nature of dependent origination.
Question: Since you have already heard the names of the fundamental dharmas of dependent origination, I do not yet know their meaning.

Answer: Within each of these three preceding gates, there are three meanings that mutually support one another. First is the meaning of having power and lacking power, by which they attain mutual penetration (*xiāngrù*).

Second is the meaning of having substance through mutual negation and sublation, by which they attain mutual identity (*xiāngjí*). Third is the meaning of the fusion of substance and function (*tǐyòng*).
It is without intrinsic meaning. By means of this, one immediately enters simultaneous sovereignty. First, regarding the characteristics of mutual entry through different aspects:

this refers to the power and function of various conditions supporting one another and mutually displacing each other; thus, there is the sense that each possesses both total power and total lack of power, and it is only in this way that dependent origination is established.
As the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* states: "That which does not arise does not arise from conditions, because it arises from its own cause. If each [condition] possessed only...
If there were no power and no lack of power, there would be the fault of multiple effects, because each [cause] would produce [its effect] individually.

If each were solely powerless and lacked power, then—just as when a single condition is missing everything fails to be accomplished—the same would apply to the others. Therefore, one [cause] is able to sustain many [effects].
First, that which possesses power can subsume the many, while the many depend upon the one. Since the many lack power, they must enter into the one;
because the one possesses power, it cannot coexist with the many who also possess power. Therefore, there is no single entity that does not subsume the many.
Because many [factors] lack power, they cannot necessarily coexist with a single factor that lacks power; therefore, there is no case where many exist without being subsumed within one.
Just as it is when one [factor] sustains many bases, so too is it when many sustain a single base. One should reflect on this by reversing the above:

regarding those that enter into the many, just as when one looks toward the many, there is the sustaining of bases which causes both powerful and powerless factors to constantly contain the many within themselves, remaining latent.
When the many exist within the one, they are simultaneously unimpeded; one should know that the same applies when the many are viewed from the perspective of the one.

The two propositions of "coexistence" and "mutual dissolution" are likewise unimpeded; this should also be understood by analogy. Regarding the meaning of the mutual identity of distinct entities, it refers to the way all conditions relate to one another.

The whole is overwhelmed; there is the sense of both having an essence and lacking an essence. Only through dependent origination is it established, for if even one condition were missing, the others would not arise.
Since arising would not be established, the meaning of conditions would be destroyed. When this one condition is obtained, the entirety of all things is established as arising.

Because they arise together, the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*) is established. Therefore, the single condition is that which brings about [the effect], while the multiple conditions and the fruit are both that which is brought about.
Thus, many [conditions] constitute a single [effect]; the many lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while the one that produces the many possesses intrinsic nature.

[The Separate Chapter says: "If the self exists at a certain time, the other must necessarily not exist. Why? Because the other is the self. Since the other lacks intrinsic nature, it is produced by the self. If the self is empty at a certain time, the other must necessarily exist. Why? Because the self is the other."

For this reason, because [a thing] lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is produced by others, another chapter states: "Many conditions, lacking intrinsic nature, constitute a single accomplishment. Therefore, the many are each individually without intrinsic nature, yet they constitute the many; thus, the existence of the many is one emptiness. Furthermore, the commentary below states: "The existence of one is the existence of all;

the negation of one is the negation of all. This is because 'all' has the meaning of emptiness; when the self is subsumed, it is the other. Because 'one' has the meaning of existence, and because it has the meaning of existence, the other is subsumed back into the self.

Thus, because "one" above has the meaning of emptiness, the self is also subsumed into the other. Because "many" has the meaning of existence, the other is subsumed back into the self. Among these four passages cited above, there are similarities and differences; reflect upon them accordingly. (This is because of the substantiality of the one.)
That which possesses multiplicity of substantiality can never coexist with that which lacks it; nor can that which lacks substantiality ever coexist with that which possesses it (one interpretation:

because a single substantial entity can encompass many, and because the absence of nature in the many is inherently identical). Therefore, there is no "one" that is not multiple, and there is no "multiple" that is not one.

As it is with the one and the multiple, so it is with the multiple and the one (reflect on this by reversing the above). Just as when viewing the one in relation to the multiple, there is substantiality and the lack of substantiality.
Therefore, one is able to subsume others within oneself and set aside oneself to identify with others;

simultaneously and without obstruction, when many are compared to one, whether they are non-existent or existent, and whether they have substance or no substance, one can likewise set aside oneself to identify with others and subsume others within oneself without any hindrance.

Thus, identifying with others while being oneself, and identifying with oneself while being others—yet not identifying with others while being oneself, nor identifying with oneself while being others—the two phrases are unobstructed, perfectly interfused, and spontaneous.
This can be seen by reflecting upon it. Regarding the principle of the dual fusion of the three bodies and their functions, and of existence and non-existence:

it means that for all conditioned phenomena (*dharmas*), they must mutually yield their power and integrate as a whole before arising through conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) can be established. Therefore, perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) also possesses six propositions.

First, because there is no essence that is not function, the entire essence is entirely function; thus, there is only function without essence, and while there is mutual inclusion (*xiang-ru*), there is no mutual identity (*xiang-jian*).
This is because: second, since there is no essence that is not function, the entire function returns to the essence, such that there is only essence and no function;

thus, while there is mutual identity (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is no mutual penetration (*anupraveśa*). Third, the function that returns to the essence does not obstruct its functioning, and the essence that is entirely function does not lose its essential nature.
Therefore, essence and function coexist without obstruction; they are both identical and penetrating, free from all hindrance.

Melted and fused in sovereign freedom: (4) the substance of total function is such that its substance vanishes; the function of total substance manifests as three. Thus, substance and function penetrate one another;
form and negation are both non-existent, being neither identical nor distinct. They share the same source in a perfect fusion of a single flavor.

(5) These five together with the preceding four lines constitute a single dependent origination, where all exist unimpededly. (6) Vanishing these five lines, they transcend dependence and leave behind words, merging in silent identity.
Regarding the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*), one should eliminate all conceptual attachments and contemplate it in accordance with reality.
This concludes the section on the gate of distinct entities. Second, as for the meaning of the mutual interpenetration of identical entities:

within the midst of manifold conditions, because a single condition must correspond to many conditions, each [condition] gives itself entirely to those many as being that one. Therefore, this one possesses many "ones. Now, these many...
First: Although it is fundamentally one, because it must correspond to many conditions, there is this "one-in-many. Nevertheless, its essence is no different from the original one;
therefore, it is called the "Gate of Identical Substance" (*samāna-svabhāva-mukha*). Furthermore, because this one must correspond to many conditions, there is this "one-in-many.
Since that which corresponds to the many conditions is mutually inclusive, this "one-in-many" is also made to be mutually inclusive. First...
This clarifies the mutual inclusion [of the one and the many]. That is to say, this single fundamental "one" possesses the power to sustain those many individual "ones";

therefore, within that single fundamental "one," those many "ones" are accommodated. The many "ones" lack independent power; they exist by depending upon the single fundamental "one. For this reason, the many "ones" enter into the single fundamental "one."
This is precisely the single fundamental [principle] that does not fail to accommodate the manifold; it is also the manifold that does not fail to enter the fundamental.

Just as the single fundamental possesses power as the sustainer while the manifold lacks power and serves as the supported, so too, in their mutual accommodation and entry, the manifold possesses power as the sustainer.

The fundamental one is without power and without support (the same applies to its capacity to contain). This means that the fundamental one contains the many ones without exception, and there is nothing among the many ones that does not enter into the fundamental one.

Thus, by viewing the many ones from the perspective of the fundamental one, because there is holding, support, power, and lack of power, it is able to contain and able to receive [the many ones] without any obstruction. When the many ones view the fundamental one, there is support...

Because they possess both powerlessness and power, they are able to enter and be contained within one another without obstruction; they both exist and are simultaneously extinguished. One should reflect accordingly upon the non-obstruction of these two phrases. Question:

What is the difference between this and the previously mentioned "different entities"? Answer: Regarding the previous case of different entities, the first [entity] looks toward the subsequent nine, such that they enter one another through different aspects (*paryāya*).
In the present case of identical entities, the ten are inherently complete within a single [entity]; it is not by looking toward [others] that they exist.

This is an explanation through different perspectives regarding what precedes and follows. (The section on the entry into the gate of the same substance is concluded. Second, the meaning of the mutual identity of the same substance:
This means that because the "one" contained within the preceding "many" also possesses both the sense of having substance and the sense of lacking substance, they are mutually identical.

Since the "one" within the many lacks substance, by virtue of the fundamental principle, the many is identical to the one. Because the fundamental "one" possesses substance and can function as the one, the one entirely subsumes the many (just as in the case where the one is many).

As it is with the many emptinesses, so it is with the one-many emptiness. A separate chapter states: "The many-ones have non-substantiality as their basis; the single manifestation of the many-ones is, in its entirety, identical to the fundamental one.

Because the fundamental one encompasses the many-ones, and because the many-ones, being devoid of substantiality, are fused into identity with the fundamental one, there is no fundamental one that does not encompass the many-ones, nor is there any many-one that is not identical to the fundamental one. This is just as the fundamental one possesses substantiality, yet [the many-ones]..."

First, regarding non-substantiality (*anātman*): since the inclusion of the many within the one is thus, so too is the inclusion of the one within the many when the many possess substantiality while the one lacks it.

Therefore, there is neither a "one" that does not include the "many," nor a "one" that is not identical to the "many. This is because when the fundamental one is viewed in relation to the many, there is both substantiality and non-substantiality;
thus, it can include others as itself and set aside itself to become identical with others. There is no [limit].
There is obstruction. For the most part, one should look back to the root. Furthermore, whether it is encompassed by essence or non-essence can be known;

likewise, whether it is encompassed or not, whether it is identity or non-identity, whether it is neither encompassed nor not encompassed, and neither identical nor non-identical—these two phrases are unimpeded. This may be seen through reflection.

(End of the section on the mutual identity of the same substance. Third, regarding the simultaneous fusion of substance and function such that one enters into non-obstruction: this also consists of six phrases of non-obstruction;
reflect upon them according to the preceding [explanation]. (End of the section on the gate of the same substance.)

Third, regarding the meaning of identity and difference between the ultimate and the conventional: because these two gates share the same dependent origination and are not mutually exclusive, if there were no distinct entities, all conditions would be confused and disordered, and thus it would not be dependent origination.
If there were no identical entity, the conditions would not support one another, and thus it would likewise not be dependent origination.
It is only through their non-confusion that they can support one another; therefore, if they were not of an identical entity, [dependent origination could not exist].

Because there is no difference in their lack of characteristics (*animitta*). If they were not of different substances, there would be no identity of substance. Therefore, a general analysis also yields four propositions:
First, some are entirely different in their essence; when fully included, they are simultaneously present. Second, some are entirely identical in their essence;

they too are fully included and simultaneously present, because phenomena are mutually pervasive and also completely encompass one another. Third, some are both, because identity and difference manifest unimpededly as a pair.
Fourth, there is that which is neither, because the characteristics cancel each other out until they are exhausted; thus, it is a double negation.
Furthermore, because the preceding various gates are collectively made into one great *pratītyasamutpāda*, many types of doctrinal gates are simultaneously and fully present.

Because abiding in one [principle] universally responds to all, there is the sovereign freedom of breadth and narrowness. Because of approaching [reality] from the perspective of essence and function, there is mutual identity and mutual inclusion.

Furthermore, when one encompasses many, it is manifest; when the entirety of one enters into many, it is hidden (the same applies to many encompassing one). Moreover, in terms of function, mutual entry is manifest;
in terms of essence, total identity is hidden (the same applies to the manifestation of identity and the concealment of entry). Furthermore, mutual entry through different aspects is manifest.

The identity of all things is hidden (the same applies when the identical is manifest and the different is hidden). Furthermore, because the meaning of mutual inclusion within the identity is subsumed by way of difference, the subtle gate is revealed.
Because the mutual inclusion of distinct entities carries within it the mutual inclusion of identical entities, there is the inexhaustible gate of the Indra’s Net of multiple layers.

Another chapter states: "The distinct natures are mutually inclusive, possessing the sense of subtlety. The characteristic of distinct natures possesses the sense of concealment and manifestation because of the mutual entry of identical natures;
thus there is the non-obstruction of the one and the many. Because identical natures are mutually identical, there is the non-obstruction of the broad and the narrow.

Furthermore, because distinct natures encompass identical natures, there is the sense of the non-obstruction of the Indra-net. (The two lines above are a marginal note. Based on this great law of dependent origination...
This is because it is the dharma-gate of the unimpeded *dharmadhātu*. There is also the dharma-gate of manifesting the Dharma by relying on phenomena (*vastu*).

Through this pervasive integration and mastery, one causes the time analyzed upon this Dharma to likewise be unimpeded and sovereign in accordance with the Dharma; hence, there is the gate of the ten periods of time.
Because these dharma-gates arise through the mutual interpenetration of a single *paratantra* dependent origination, whenever any one gate is present, they are all identical.

Because they arise through mutual conditioning, whenever one gate is present, all others are necessarily complete. Thus, this is the Gate of Principal and Retinue (the section above concludes the Gate of Mutual Dependence of the Characteristics of Dependent Origination).
The three sections for investigating the profound meaning (*tanyuan yi*) are the same as before.
First, regarding the explanation of the names: the ocean of meaning is profoundly deep, transcending the realm of conceptual thought and being inconceivable;

therefore, it is called "profound" (*xuan*). One investigates and grasps to reveal its intent; therefore, it is called "investigating" (*tan*). Because there is a profound underlying reason, it is called "meaning" (*yi*).
Second, regarding the determination of its essence: it takes the unobstructed *dharmadhātu* as its essence. Master Huiyuan states that there are two kinds of essential entities (*vastu*):

first, that which is purely immaculate and untainted (*anāsrava*), which is the essential entity upon which the characteristics of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*) depend; second, that which is both tainted and untainted, which is the essential entity upon which functional activity (*karma-vṛtti*) depends.
This refers to the ten dharmas—form, mind, time, place, body, direction, teaching, meaning, practice, and stage—which are cited here to provide a comprehensive analysis.
The first two [sections] are as previously explained (*yúnyún*).
The third consists of questions and answers for detailed analysis. Question: Since it is said that [this reality] transcends the realm of the emotions (*chúqíng*), how can it be known?

Answer: Master Fǎzàng says that ten gates are briefly cited to encompass its essential principles: namely, first, the gate of simultaneous and perfect mutual correspondence; second, the gate of... [the text continues with further gates].
1. The Gate of Narrowness, Sovereignty, and Non-obstruction; 2. The Gate of the Mutual Inclusion of One and Many Without Confusion; 3. The Gate of the Sovereign Interpenetration of All Dharmas; 4.
The Gate of the Simultaneous Accomplishment of the Hidden and the Manifest; 5. The Gate of the Microscopic Inclusion and Stable Establishment; 6. The Gate of the Indra’s Net Dharma-realm; 7.
The Gate of Revealing the Dharma through Phenomena to Generate Understanding; 8. The Gate of the Distinctness of Dharmas Across the Ten Ages.

The Section on Accomplishment. The tenth is the Gate of the Perfect Clarity and Endowment of Principal and Retinue. Now, these ten gates share a single *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination); they are unimpeded and perfectly interfused.
One should reflect that with the presence of any single gate, all others are fully contained within it. Within the first gate, there is the fulfillment of ten meanings:
first, the fulfillment of teaching and meaning; second, principle and phenomenon; third, object and wisdom; fourth, practice and stage; fifth, cause and difference.
Sixth, the reliance on the primary and secondary [realms]. Seventh, essence and function. Eighth, persons and dharmas. Ninth, the inverse and the conformative. Tenth, response and stimulus.

When these ten aforementioned factors are fully present and simultaneously correspond, they constitute a single *pratītyasamutpāda*. There is no sequence of before and after, nor any distinction such as "end" and so forth;
each single factor possesses all other meanings. Interwoven yet not confused, they form the limit of dependent origination. Master Huiyuan said: "This gate serves as..."
The former is the general; the latter nine are the specific.

Regarding the second point, the non-obstruction between the broad and the narrow: because differentiation is itself non-differentiation, and non-differentiation is itself differentiation, they are unimpeded and sovereign.
Just as a single atom universally pervades the entire dharma-realm without destroying its original position, so too, this may be exclusively vast and unobstructed;
or it may have distinct boundaries; or it may be both vast and narrow; or it may be such that both vastness and narrowness are extinguished;

or it may possess all four of these states, because it is the realm of understanding. Or it may transcend all four of these, because it is the realm of practice (the same applies to all subsequent cases).

Regarding the gate of the mutual compatibility of the one, three, and many: this single dharma, having expanded itself, universally enters into all dharmas, thereby encompassing them all and causing them to enter within itself.
Expansion and inclusion occur simultaneously; since there is no obstruction, a verse in this sutra says:
"With a single buddha-land filling the ten directions, the ten directions enter into one without remainder; yet the original characteristics of the worlds are not destroyed."

It is because of incomparable merit that it is thus able to do so. (Master Huiyuan says: These six phrases are viewed in relation to the one and the many—namely, one within one, many within many, many within one, one within many, many within one, and one-many within one-many;
the remaining cases of great and small, etc., are to be understood by analogy).

Fourth, regarding the gate of the mutual identity of the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa-paramārtha-samanta-mukha*): this means that within this single phenomenon, setting aside its own self-nature, it is identical with others;

its entire substance is entirely those other all-encompassing phenomena. Yet, it constantly subsumes others to be identical with itself, such that the entirety of those all-encompassing phenomena is precisely its own substance.

Thus, the one and the many are mutually identical, merging without obstruction. As the Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva who has first resolved for enlightenment is himself the Buddha. Based on this condition...

It arises. From its beginning to its end, the wondrous principle is entirely equal to suchness; thus one attains the ultimate consummation. Only through the end does one return to the origin. It is further said:
"Abiding in a single stage, one universally encompasses the merits of all stages. Therefore, by attaining one, one attains all.
Furthermore, it is said: "Because one knows that the one is many and the many are one. This refers precisely to the case of attaining Buddhahood at the final stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Regarding the statement within the "Gate of Identical Substance" (*tongti yimen*) that "the one encompasses all inexhaustible phenomena," does this mean they manifest simultaneously, or sequentially?
Answer: Within a single gate, all things manifest brilliantly and simultaneously.
That which is subsumed under the gateway of subtlety manifests in layers of mutual interpenetration.

That which is subsumed under the gateway of Indra (the net of Indra) means that all other meanings are simultaneously identical and different, many and few, existent and non-existent, beginning and end.
Thus, one possesses sovereign mastery over all inexhaustible dharma-gates; yet whichever is raised as the primary subject, the others serve as its companions. The principle is one and not two.
[This is] a discrepancy; it has been so from the beginning. Question: If all things are already fully contained within a single gate, what is the use of the other gates?
Answer: The other gates are like space. Why is this? Because within a single gate of identical essence, everything is simultaneously subsumed without exception.
Question: Regarding "everything subsumed" within this identical essence, does it refer only to everything within its own gate?

Can it possibly encompass all things within the other gates? Answer: Since it encompasses all within its own [gate], there is nothing remaining when it subsequently encompasses each and every one of the other gates.
Why is this? Because within the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*, neither "one" nor "all" can be established as such.
This is because we are here discussing only the actual virtues of the *dharmadhātu* family; thus, its boundaries and measure cannot be stated. As a verse in this sutra says:
Throughout unspeakable eons, one may expound all that is unspeakable;

yet while such unspeakable eons might come to an end, the exposition of the unspeakable can never be exhausted. Furthermore, a verse says: "The minds of all sentient beings may all be distinguished and known;
even the number of atoms in all lands may be calculated; the realm of empty space in the ten directions may still be measured by a single hair."

Regarding the measure [of the Bodhisattva’s resolve]: the initial aspiration of a Bodhisattva is ultimately unfathomable. This is because, through the Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), by attaining one, one attains all;
thus cause and effect are simultaneous, as there is no distinction between priority and posteriority. The *Dilun* states:
"The Bodhisattva at the stage of faith, up to the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, constitute a single dependent origination through the six aspects of totality and particularity."

One should grasp this meaning by applying it: clearly understand that cause and effect exist simultaneously, are mutually inclusive and identical, each encompassing all things, and function as both principal and attendant to one another.
One must contemplate this deeply; there is no doubt regarding this matter. Furthermore, it is said:

"At the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening, fully endowed with the body of wisdom, not through realization dependent on others" (and so forth, in immeasurable detail). Question: These passages merely praise the virtues within the causal stage; how could they possibly [refer to anything else]?
"Can this be the fruition-merit itself? Answer: "This is the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Cause and fruit are of the same essence, forming a single dependent origination.
To attain this is to attain that, because they are mutually identical. If the fruit were not attained, the cause would not be established as a cause.
Why? Because without attaining the fruit, it is not a cause. Question: "In various places, the aspect of the fruit cannot be spoken of; only the cause is taught."
As for the division: why is it that at the final stage of the Ten Faiths, one distinguishes the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood?
The answer is that "becoming a Buddha" refers to the fact that from the initial stage of seeing and hearing onwards, up until the second birth, one accomplishes the practice of Buddhahood.
When the causal stage is fully perfected at the final mind-moment, in the third birth, one immediately attains that ultimate, sovereign, and perfectly integrated fruit. This is because...
Because the substance of the cause is established in dependence upon the fruit, once the cause is fulfilled, it is subsumed within the ocean of the fruit.
Since this is the realm of realization, it cannot be described in words.

This is as explained extensively in the sutras regarding the cases of the Dragon Girl, the youth Samantavyūha, Sudhana, the Devaputra Tuṣitaka, and others, who attained that very fruit within three lifetimes.

[The Master] Distinguished [the teachings]. Question: It was stated above that one becomes a Buddha in a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*). Since this principle already exists within the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), how does it differ from this? Answer:
In the Three Vehicles, with respect to the ultimate principle (*li*), one becomes a Buddha in a single thought-moment.

However, in this One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), in a single thought-moment, one simultaneously attains the full realization of all teachings, meanings, principles, phenomena, causes, effects, persons, dharmas, and so forth; all are entirely simultaneous. Simultaneous.

(Regarding the ten stages of) becoming a Buddha: yet this single thought-moment is no different from hundreds of thousands of kalpas. One should reflect upon this. As for the fifth, the Gate of the Hidden and the Manifest:
it means that when one encompasses many, the one is manifest and the many are hidden; when all encompass one, the one is hidden and the many are manifest.

The manifestation of the many does not coexist with the hiddenness of the one, nor do the hiddennesses of the many occur simultaneously. Thus, the hidden and the manifest, and the manifest and the hidden, occur at the same time.
There is no obstruction. As the Sūtra says: "Entering meditative absorption (samāpatti) here, one arises from samādhi in another direction;

entering meditative absorption through the faculty of the eye, one arises from samādhi regarding the object of form (rūpa-dhātu). This is like ten coins within the first coin being called "manifest," whereas those same ten coins are "hidden" in relation to the first coin.
Why? Because when one sees this, one does not see that; they do not [simultaneously]...
Because they are known as such, although they do not see one another, what is established here is precisely what is established there; thus, it is called "simultaneous establishment.

Sixth is the gate of the subtle mutual containment: all these aforementioned meanings—the beginning and end, identity and difference, priority and posteriority, direct and reverse order, and so forth—all such dharma-gates manifest simultaneously and vividly within a single thought-moment, appearing clearly and without exception.
This is because, like the arrow of the Tathāgata, they appear simultaneously and fully manifest. As the Sūtra says:
"In a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva manifests everything from descending from Tuṣita Heaven and entering the womb, up until the dissemination of his relics. It further states:
"Within a single atom, there are subtle lands, adorned and pure, dwelling therein in vast serenity. (One should contemplate this according to the principle.)
The seventh is the gate of Indra’s net. This means that within each and every atom, there is universally manifested an ocean of boundless lands.
Within those oceans of lands, there are further atoms; within those atoms, there are again oceans of lands.
Thus, they are layered upon one another in an inexhaustible manner, beyond the reach of mental calculation or intellectual speculation, just like the net of Śakra, Lord of Devas.
The brilliance of the jewels is so transparent that they reflect one another, and these reflections appear again and again without end. As the sutra says:
"It is like the world-systems of Indra’s net," and it further says: "Within a single atom, each manifests countless billions of nayutas of Buddhas."
Within that [single atom], he preaches the Dharma (*jñānasambuddha-loka*). Within a single atom, he manifests immeasurable Buddha-lands, Mount Sumeru, and the Cakravāḍa mountains;

yet the world is not cramped (*bhājana-loka*). Within a single atom, he manifests the three evil realms, devas, and asuras, each experiencing their respective karmic retributions (*sattva-loka*). Furthermore, it says: "All Buddha-fields, atoms..."

As many Buddhas as there are atoms [in the world], they sit within a single pore, each surrounded by an immeasurable assembly of Bodhisattvas, who individually and fully expound the practices of Samantabhadra.
Immeasurable oceans of lands reside within a single hair; all are seated upon lotus thrones of enlightenment, pervading all dharma-realms.
These appear with sovereign mastery from every single pore. Furthermore, it is said: "Just as is manifested within a single minute atom..."
"All atoms are likewise [as previously described]... (and so forth). These are all actual realities (*bhūta-artha*) and are not produced through transformation.

This refers to the objects of the *yathā-mātra* (conformity with reality) within the *yathā-buddhi* (wisdom as it is). Other instances of transformational manifestations do not fall under this category. Why is this?
Because these are the actual virtues of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), which are such by their very nature; they are not objects of conceptualized mental construction.

(One may dispel such conceptual thoughts. He asked the Master: "Regarding the statement that 'within a single atom, immeasurable lands are manifested' and so forth—this is merely a single layer of manifestation.
How can it be considered a 'layered' [manifestation]? The Master replied: "This is precisely when the *Avataṃsaka* is being taught;
within all atoms, it is likewise so. When the *Avataṃsaka* is being taught within those minute atoms, it is also said that within all atoms, it is likewise being taught in this same way."
Layer upon layer, infinitely and inexhaustibly. Question: According to this text, if there are infinite layers, what is their limit?
How can one distinguish their beginning, end, and so forth? Answer: It depends on how the wisdom perceives them. Taking one as the primary, the rest become its companions.
From the perspective of that which is primary, it is called the "central" [element], while the rest are its retinue. This extends throughout the entire *Indra-jāla* (net) of the Dharma-realm.
[The Master] Luo Cheng also asked: "Regarding this meaning, how does it differ from the 'subtle' (weixi) mentioned above? [The Master] replied:

"That which manifests with its entirety clearly apparent is subsumed under the 'subtle' (weixi), wherein the multilayered [realms] appear in mutual concealment and reflection. This is subsumed under the 'Indra's Net' (yintuoluo).
These various meanings are each distinct and not the same; you should reflect upon them carefully."

Regarding the eighth, the gate of revealing the Dharma by relying on phenomena (*dharmaparyāya-ālambana-dharmamukha*): this means that seeing these phenomena is itself seeing the inexhaustible dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

It is not that one relies on these phenomena to signify something else entirely. As the Sūtra says: "These flower-canopies and so forth arise from the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)," and so on.
Question: Since this principle exists within the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), how does it differ from this [Mahāyāna] teaching? Answer: In the Three Vehicles, one relies on different phenomena.

Regarding "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): they manifest and appear as distinct phenomena. Now, these phenomenal characteristics upon which this One Vehicle relies are none other than the principles they manifest;
there is no difference between them. It fully encompasses all matters of principle and phenomena, as well as teachings and meanings, such that nothing is left uncontained.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Ten Intervals of Time (*daśa-kāla-antarāya-dharmamukha*): the various meanings mentioned above pervade all phenomena and encompass all time.
That is to say, the three periods of each of the three times are subsumed into a single thought-moment; thus, there are ten times.
Since time has no separate substance and is established based upon phenomena, as phenomena are unimpeded, so too is time. As the Sūtra says: "All past kalpas are placed..."

The future and the present; future kalpas are transposed into the past world-age. It is further said that immeasurable kalpas are but a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment is immeasurable kalpas, and so forth.
It is also said that one may enter short kalpas by means of long kalpas, or enter long kalpas by means of short kalpas.
A kalpa with a Buddha enters a kalpa without a Buddha; a kalpa without a Buddha enters a kalpa with a Buddha, and so forth. (As stated above...
All these aforementioned meanings are freely manifested within the ten periods of time because they constitute the dependent origination; thus, one attains immediate entry.
The tenth is the Gate of the Perfect Clarity of Principal and Retinue. This teaching of the Perfect [Dharmadhātu] does not arise in isolation;

its principle necessitates that the principal and the retinue arise together. As the Sūtra says: "This great lotus has as many accompanying flowers as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds. It further states:
"The Prince Mahātejas (in the Jin translation, the Youth Samalaṃkāra) heard the Buddha preach the *Sarvadharma-dhātu-vimala-alaṃkāra-sūtra*."
There are as many sūtras as there are atoms in a world-system that serve as its retinue. Furthermore, it is like one direction acting as the principal and the ten directions acting as its companions;
the same applies to all other directions. For this reason, the principals do not see one another, nor do the companions see one another;

yet, whether principal or companion, they are perfectly luminous and endowed with all virtues. Moreover, there are two meanings to this: first, those of the same class; second, those of different classes. Regarding the first, those of the same class:
As it is said regarding the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields from each of the ten directions come to bear witness.

They are all named Dharmamati, and in the presence of Buddhas such as myself, they likewise preach the Ten Abodes. The assembly of followers, the names, phrases, and syllables are identical and without difference.
Therefore, one should know that for each of the Ten Abodes, there are as many sūtras as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.

...and so forth, taking these as their retinues. Just as in the first *daśabhūmi*, all other instances of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) taught in every location likewise comprise retinues numbering as many as atoms.

Since this is the case for the ten stages, it should be understood through the same interpretation that each of the other assemblies—such as the ten practices (*daśacaryā*)—possesses a specific quantity of realized dharmas.
Second, regarding "different types": this refers to considering a single direction or a single realm as one type.

As for the *kī* (the responsive teaching): it expounds the Dharma in a single assembly; since it concludes by universally extending its discourse to the ten directions and so forth, it is not the primary scripture (*mūlasūtra*).
Nevertheless, because it serves as a superior expedient means for the primary scripture, it constitutes its retinue (*parivāra*).

Therefore, while the primary scriptures necessarily expound the same teaching simultaneously across the dust-motes of the ten directions, the accompanying scriptures (*sahāyasūtra*) are not thus; they differ according to each region. Consequently, each primary scripture has a retinue as numerous as the dust-motes.

Furthermore, within the ancient commentaries (*śāstra*), there are explained the "Gate of the Pure and Mixed Virtues of the Various Treasuries" (*piṭaka*) and the "Gate of the Perfect Accomplishment through the Revolving of Mind-Only.
The categories of meaning (*artha-mukha*) are infinite and cannot be fully set forth here.
Regarding the meanings and so forth elucidated in the ten gates above: they share a single dependent origination that is unimpeded and perfectly interfused.

Whichever gate one encounters, it immediately encompasses all others; this should be contemplated. Just as it is with the first gate, so it is with the remaining nine gates—such as the broad and the narrow—which each individually possess the ten preceding periods;
they differ only according to their respective gates. Therefore, within each and every gate, there are hundreds of thousands.

Reflecting upon this, it becomes clear. (That is to say, for example, if a single doctrinal category (*dharma*) carries its own ten meanings and possesses these ten gates, there are one hundred [categories]. Other doctrinal categories and so forth should each be calculated accordingly; thus, they form a thousand gates.

For instance, when doctrinal categories and the like are compared to their own ten meanings and the ten simultaneous gates, these constitute the thousand gates. One should reflect that those "simultaneous" factors and others, when compared to their own ten gates and doctrinal categories and so forth, likewise constitute a thousand gates.)
The three sections on the meaning of the Universal Dharma (Pufa) are the same as before.
First, regarding the explanation of the names: "Pu" means "broad" (*prabhūta*). It signifies the sense of pervasiveness; this is "Universal.

"Dharma" has the sense of self-nature and the sense of a rule or standard (*lakṣaṇa*), as is commonly explained. This refers to the mutual entry of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas. Regarding the term "mutual entry," Xiao says: it means that one...
All worlds enter into a single atom; a single atom enters into all worlds (as it is for one atom, so it is for all).
All kalpas of the three periods of time enter into a single kṣaṇa; a single kṣaṇa enters into the kalpas of the three periods of time (as it is for one kṣaṇa, so it is for all).
Just as the great and the small mutually enter one another, so it is with all other gates of mutual entry. It is also the same as what was said regarding their characteristics, namely:
All phenomena and all gateways—this oneness is the one; this oneness is thus vast and pervasive, and is called the Universal Dharma (sarvadharma).
Second, regarding the establishment of its essence: it takes the unobstructed dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as its essence.
The third section: Questions and Answers on Differentiation. Question: By what causes and conditions do these various phenomena attain such mutual interpenetration and non-obstruction?
Answer: Master Fazang states that the causes and conditions are immeasurable and difficult to enumerate in full; here, ten categories are presented to explain this non-obstruction:
1. Because there is no fixed limit to the great and the small; 2. Because each is manifested solely by the mind; 3. Because they are unreal, like illusions; ... [and so forth].

Therefore: (1) because it arises from four infinite causes; (2) because of the mastery of supreme supernormal powers; (3) because of the great function of samādhi; (4) because of the inconceivable exposition;
(5) because the qualities of the fruit are perfectly consummate; (6) because of the mutual dependence of dependent origination;
(7) because the nature of phenomena is harmoniously integrated. Master Wonhyo said: "To speak briefly, there are ten kinds of causes: first, one with one..."
1. All things act as mutual reflections for one another, like the net of Indra (*indrajāla*). 2. One and all arise through mutual conditioning and aggregation, like the counting of coins.
3. All are nothing but consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), like the objects of a dream. 4. All lack substantial reality, like magical illusions (*māyā*). 5.
Their common characteristics differ because they pervade all things. 6. From the greatest to the smallest, they are all equal and uniform.

7. Because it is the measure (pramāṇa). 8. Because the dharmatā of dependent origination is free from [inherent] nature. 9. Because the essence of the single mind-dharma is neither one nor different. 10.
Because the unobstructed dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) has neither limit nor center. 11. Because the dharma-realm is suchness (dharmatā), being without obstruction or hindrance.
The two masters mentioned above each have ten gates; although their expositions are extensive and detailed, we shall now take the first [set] from Master Zang.
The sixth section, by Master Menxiao, reveals its essential principles. Master Fazang said: "The great is not fixed as great, and thus it can enter the small;

the small is not fixed as small, and thus it can contain the great. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Mount Vajra-parikhā is immeasurable in number, yet all can be placed upon the tip of a single hair.
If one wishes to know how the ultimate great possesses a small aspect, the Bodhisattva begins from this point."
"Generating the mind. The commentary explains: herein it is clarified that because the "great" is not truly great, there is the appearance of the "small.

Question: When the world enters a minute particle and Mount Sumeru enters a mustard seed, since there are already forms of "great" and "small," how can they be mutually contained without the small increasing or the great decreasing?
Answer: Regarding the principle of emptiness, it is said that conventional reality is illusory and false; [the ultimate truth is] superior...

The ultimate meaning is fundamentally empty. When one is deluded by the false and provisional, the mind becomes obstructed; thus, the small and the great are separated by barriers. When one awakens to the nature of illusion, the mind becomes pervasive—how could they not then be mutually inclusive?

Moreover, since the vast disparity between the great and the small arises from the deluded attachment to existence, once one realizes the supreme truth of emptiness, what obstruction would prevent them from being permeated by it?

(This is the position of Bhāviveka. The *Yogācāra-tattvaviniścaya* states that there are briefly eight explanations. First, regarding the attachment to an object of attachment, the great and the small are vastly separated.

First, regarding the emptiness of what is grasped: how can one know whether it is small or great? Second, failing to realize the dependent nature—that is, that the essence of "true" greatness or smallness is illusory—what principle remains uncomprehended?

Third, if the three natures constitute greatness or smallness, perhaps they cannot accommodate one another; yet the perfected nature is all-pervasive and harmonious, so why would they not be mutually inclusive?

Fourth, if one clings to dharmas as having functional utility, then greatness and smallness will be contradictory; but if one knows that dharmas arise from causes and conditions and are equally empty, how could they not be harmonized?

1. When the five delusions cause the mind to cling to objects, who can tolerate the existence of real objects? Upon awakening, one realizes that all objects are consciousness; what, then, cannot be attained? 2.
If dharmas truly possessed characteristics, there would be no room for "great" or "small. Since non-characteristic (*animitta*) is the truth, what could be great and what could be small? 3.

As long as one has not yet accorded with True Suchness (*tathatā*), the ignorant mind remains profoundly separated from it. Only by knowing the true and penetrating the false can wisdom thoroughly achieve mastery. 4. The ordinary minds of those in lower stations cannot comprehend or contain this.
"What can the spiritual power of this Superior Man (*upari-pudgala*) not accomplish? (This is the school that protects the Dharma. Master Wonhyo said: First, the Southern School says:
'Since it is called "inconceivable," it is solely the realm of the Sages; the Two Vehicles cannot fathom it, so how could ordinary people understand it?
